articles.headline: Meningitis Cases in Ghana
articles.summary: Ghana continues to grapple with meningitis, predominantly in the Northern, Upper East and Upper West Regions, where the disease is endemic and outbreaks occur mainly during the dry season (November–April). From 1998–2021 there were over 71,000 suspected cases and about 3,865 confirmed cases; case fatality historically ranges from 20% to 47%, with some outbreaks reaching 36%–50%. In 2025, the Upper West Region reported about 269 suspected cases and 36 confirmed cases with several deaths; the Upper East Region had 31 suspected cases with confirmed deaths. Seasonal surveillance January–March shows rising case numbers. High-prevalence districts reach up to 54%, while Greater Accra and Ashanti remain low (often <5%). Most cases are bacterial meningitis caused by Streptococcus pneumoniae (most common), Neisseria meningitidis, and Haemophilus influenzae. Those most affected are children and young adults (5–29); males slightly more than females. Vaccination (e.g., MenAfriVac), surveillance, and prompt antibiotic treatment reduce deaths.

articles.headline: GROWING FATALITIES FROM LASSA FEVER The authorities could do more to contain the scourge
articles.summary: Lassa fever in Nigeria: 109 deaths in the first nine weeks of 2026, with about 37 health workers infected (six in one week). Across 18 states in 69 LGAs, at least one confirmed case; predominant in Bauchi, Ondo, Taraba, Benue and Edo. Incubation 6–21 days; initial symptoms fever and weakness, then headache, sore throat, nausea, vomiting, cough, and bleeding from mouth or nose. Diagnosis is challenging due to non-specific symptoms. Transmission from exposure to food or items contaminated with rat urine or faeces; prevention advice includes covering food, handwashing, clearing home surroundings, and keeping doors/windows closed at night. WHO cites reduced surveillance and lab testing contributing to high fatality; late presentation and treatment costs worsen outcomes. Experts urge stronger, coordinated prevention and long-term measures by federal and state authorities. Lassa fever is endemic in Benin Republic, Ghana, Sierra Leone; first identified in Lassa, Borno State (1969).

articles.headline: CEPI 3.0 and the Race to Develop the World's First Lassa Fever Vaccine - Nigeria Health Watch
articles.summary: Lassa fever remains Nigeria’s seasonal public health burden, with Edo State’s Irrua Specialist Teaching Hospital and Ondo State’s Federal Medical Centre at Owo repeatedly treating cases as the dry season returns. Nigeria accounts for the highest West African confirmed cases; across the region an estimated 100,000–300,000 infections occur annually, and more than 1,500 Lassa-related deaths occurred 2018–2025. Transmission is mainly via contact with food or household items contaminated by infected rodents; data show rising confirmed cases over eight years, aided by improved surveillance and diagnostics. Vaccine development is accelerating: the rVSVΔG-LASV-GPC candidate (IAVI, CEPI) is in Phase 2 in West Africa (Nigeria, Ghana, Liberia); the Oxford ChAdOx1 Lassa vaccine is in early Phase 1, first volunteer in 2025. CEPI 3.0 launched in Feb 2026 as a five-year plan with the 100 Days Mission; three priorities are listed, starting with accelerating vaccines for known high‑risk pathogens; the article truncates the rest.
